numberedLines.text: The bus went as far as the caravan park and stopped, because after that there is nowhere
to turn round. From the shelter it was two miles of sea wall, with the marsh on my left
going the colour of a bruise as the afternoon got on.
I had been meaning to walk out to Saltmere for about four years. Twice I had got as far
as the caravan park.
Nan calls it the chapel, although there is no chapel on the map and no name printed
anywhere near it. Her mother was born out there in a row of four cottages. By the time
Nan was my age there were two of them left, and now there is a step that goes down into
water and a piece of wall with the shape of a window in it. That is the story I have had
all my life, told slightly differently each time. Some years the sea came in one night
in February and took the lot. Some years it took forty years about it, a bit at a go,
and everybody watched it happen and moved their furniture up the hill.
The photograph was the reason I was out there. Nan has been at Fern Court since March
and there is nothing on her wall but a calendar from the surgery, so I said I would get
her a picture of the place. I could not tell you which visit I said it on. She agrees
with most things now, the way you agree with the radio.
I had told Mum I was going to Ryan's.
The wall is only a bank of earth with a path worn along the top of it, and the further
out you go the less anybody has bothered with it. There were sheep on the landward side
and hardly any grass for them. Below me a boat lay in the mud with its ribs showing
through and a gull standing on it, and further along, a half mile of posts went out into
the channel in a line, black and leaning, like the last of something that used to be a
bridge.
About halfway along, the wind dropped out of my ears and I could hear how much water
there was. It sat behind the bank on my right, shifting itself about, higher up than the
field I was walking beside. I kept going and did not look over for a while.
The birds went up twice. Both times it was because of me.
Saltmere, when I got to it, was smaller than any version of the story. The step is
there. The wall is there, about as high as a wheelie bin, with an elder growing out of
the top and the window-shape you can put your arm through. Somebody had been out before
me and left a can in the grass. I picked it up because it seemed rude not to, and then
had nowhere to put it, so I carried it round with me, which spoiled the effect.
I stood on the step. The water came up over the toe of my boot and went out again. I
moved back, and a minute later it came further up, and I understood it was not going to
stop doing that for me.
Nan says you can hear the bell out there when the tide turns. I stood still long enough
to be sure. There is a buoy in the channel that knocks when the water moves, a flat
sound with nothing musical in it, and I decided that was what she had always meant, and
that she knew it.
The light was going, and the marsh behind me had gone from bruise to no colour at all. I
got the phone out. I had to hold it in both hands, and even then the picture came out
grey and shaken along one edge where my hand had moved. It has the elder in it and about
half the window. I have not sent it to anybody. I put the phone back in my pocket and
started counting the posts the other way.

stem.text: Look at lines 1 to 3. Why does the bus stop at the caravan park?

rows.key: Because there is nowhere for it to turn round.

options.value: Because there is nowhere for it to turn round.
Because that is as far as he had ever got before.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: True of him at line 5, and it is not why the bus turns back.

options.value: Because nobody lives any further out than that.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The passage never says who lives out there, only that cottages once did.

options.value: Because the two miles of sea wall begin there.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 1 gives the reason outright: the bus has no way of turning round.

rows.hintCore: The sentence gives its own reason. Read past the comma.
rows.walkScript: Start at line 1 and read to the comma. The reason comes straight after because. It is about the road, not about him. Line 5 is a different fact altogether.

stem.text: Read lines 4 and 5. What do they say about Saltmere and this walk?

rows.key: He got as far as the caravan park, twice.

options.value: He got as far as Saltmere, twice.
options.tagChildHint: Two answers can look almost the same. Find what differs and check it against the text.
options.execution: One word out: line 5 says the caravan park, which is where the bus stops.

options.value: He got as far as the caravan park, twice.
He had never set out for Saltmere before.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: Line 5 says twice, so never is stronger than the passage.

options.value: He walked out to Saltmere about four years ago.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 4 gives four years of meaning to go, not a visit four years back.

rows.hintCore: Two numbers here. One is years, one is attempts.
rows.walkScript: Read line 4, then line 5. One gives how long he has meant to go. The other gives how far he actually got. Twice is the number that matters.

stem.text: Read lines 13 to 15. Why did he want a photograph of the place?

rows.key: Nan's wall has nothing on it but a calendar.

options.value: Nan asked him to bring her back a picture.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Line 15 has him say he would get her one; the offer is his.

options.value: He cannot remember which visit he promised it on.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: True at line 15, and it is about the promise rather than the reason for it.

options.value: Nan's wall has nothing on it but a calendar.
He wanted a picture of Saltmere for himself.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Lines 13 to 15 put the picture on her wall, and say nothing about his own.

rows.hintCore: Find the bare wall. The reason is what would go on it.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 14 and find what is on her wall. One calendar, from the surgery. That is the gap the picture is meant to fill. The date in line 13 answers a different question.

stem.text: Read lines 15 to 17. What do these lines tell you about the trip?

rows.key: He kept the trip from his mother.

options.value: His mother would have stopped him going.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: The passage never gives her a view on it; only that he did not tell her.

options.value: He had promised Nan he would go out there.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Line 15 has him promise a picture, not a visit; the promise moves to the wrong thing.

options.value: His mother told him to go round to Ryan's.
options.tagChildHint: Ask who is doing it and who it is being done to.
options.execution: Line 17 runs the other way: he is the one doing the telling.

options.value: He kept the trip from his mother.

rows.hintCore: One line, no reason given. Ask who was told what.
rows.walkScript: Read line 17 on its own. It sits apart from everything around it. He tells his mother one place and goes to another. Nothing explains it, and that is the point.

stem.text: Read lines 18 to 23. What lies in the mud below the wall?

rows.key: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.

options.value: A boat with its ribs showing, and a gull on it.
A half mile of black posts leaning into the channel.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 21 puts those further along, not below him in the mud.

options.value: What is left of an old bridge across the channel.
options.tagChildHint: Figures of speech are not facts. Ask what the words are really saying.
options.execution: Line 22 says the posts are LIKE the last of a bridge; no bridge is stated.

options.value: The remains of a row of four cottages.
options.tagChildHint: A true fact from somewhere else does not answer this question. Find the part the question points to.
options.execution: The cottages are real, at line 7, and they are out at Saltmere, not here.

rows.hintCore: One word fixes the place. Find below, and stop there.
rows.walkScript: Go to line 20 and find the word below. What follows it is the answer. Read on to line 21 and notice further along, which moves you somewhere else. The posts are that somewhere else.

stem.text: Read lines 24 to 26. Why does he keep from looking over at the water?

rows.key: It sat higher up than the field beside him.

options.value: He was in a hurry to reach Saltmere before dark.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Nothing in these lines rushes him; line 26 has him simply keeping going.

options.value: It sat higher up than the field beside him.
The wind was blowing hard into his eyes.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Line 24 says the wind dropped out of his ears, so it had eased, not risen.

options.value: He looked over as soon as he could hear the water.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 26 says he did not look over for a while, and this loses that.

rows.hintCore: Work out where the water is compared with him.
rows.walkScript: Read lines 25 and 26 together: the words higher up than the field straddle them. The water is behind the bank, above the field he walks beside. Line 26 gives what he does about that.

stem.text: Look at lines 28 to 30. Line 29 puts an 'elder' on top of the wall. What is an 'elder' here?

options.value: an older member of the family
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: A real sense of the word, and line 29 has this one growing out of the wall.

options.value: the hole shaped like a window
options.tagChildHint: This word is joined to another one. Work out which of the two the question is asking about before you answer.
options.execution: That is the other thing on the wall at line 30, joined to this one by and.

options.value: a small tree or bush

rows.hintCore: One word here is doing something only a plant can do.
rows.walkScript: Read line 29 and find the words growing out of. Only a plant does that. The wall carries two things, joined by and. This is the one that grows.

stem.text: Look at lines 31 and 32. On line 32 the can he is carrying 'spoiled the effect'. What does he mean by 'the effect'?

rows.key: the feeling of the visit he was making

options.value: what picking the can up led to
options.tagChildHint: You know one meaning for this word. Check that meaning fits what the sentence is saying here.
options.execution: A real sense of the word, and here it is a feeling being spoiled, not a result.

options.value: the trouble of carrying a can round with him
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 32 has him carrying it, and the carrying is what does the spoiling.

options.value: that it seemed rude not to pick it up
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: Reuses line 31 word for word, and says nothing about what the word means.

options.value: the feeling of the visit he was making

rows.hintCore: Ask what a can in your hand ruins. Not a result.
rows.walkScript: Read line 31 to the end of line 32. He picks up a can and then carries it round. Ask what carrying it round would spoil for him. It is a mood rather than a result.

stem.text: Read lines 10 to 12, then lines 33 to 35. What does standing on the step settle about Nan's story?

rows.key: The story has two speeds, but the water he watches is the slow one.

options.value: The story has two speeds, but the water he watches is the slow one.
The sea took the whole row in one night in February, as she says.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: That is the other version, at line 11, and the step shows the slow one instead.

options.value: None of what Nan has told him about the place ever really happened.
options.tagChildHint: Does the passage really go that far? Check the strongest word in the option.
options.execution: Line 33 has him standing on the step, so at least that much of it is real.

options.value: The water comes up, but then leaves the step alone.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Line 34 says it was not going to stop, and this option loses that.

rows.hintCore: The story offers two speeds. Ask which one the step shows.
rows.walkScript: Read line 11 and find the two versions: one night, or forty years. Now read line 34. The water comes up, goes out, and comes further up. That is the slow version happening while he stands there.

stem.text: Read lines 36 to 39. What makes the sound Nan calls the bell?

rows.key: A buoy in the channel, knocking as the water moves.

options.value: A bell in the chapel that went under the sea years ago.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 6 says there is no chapel on the map, and no bell appears anywhere.

options.value: A buoy in the channel, knocking as the water moves.
A sound with a clear musical note to it.
options.tagChildHint: A negative word can change the whole answer. Read the line again for one.
options.execution: Lines 37 and 38 say there is nothing musical in it, and this loses that.

options.value: The turning of the tide in the channel.
options.tagChildHint: Being in the lines is not enough. Check it answers the question you were asked.
options.execution: Line 36 gives the turning tide as when the sound comes, not as what makes it.

rows.hintCore: Something in the channel makes the sound. Find what.
rows.walkScript: Look at line 37 and find the buoy. It knocks when the water moves. Line 38 tells you what that sound is like. He then decides this is what she meant.

stem.text: Read lines 40 to 42. Why did the picture come out grey and shaken?

rows.key: The light had gone and his hands would not hold still.

options.value: The wind shook the phone as he held it.
options.tagChildHint: Ask what exactly made this happen. Re-read the moment step by step.
options.execution: Line 41 gives the movement to his own hand, not to any wind.

options.value: There was something the matter with the camera on his phone.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Lines 40 and 41 give the light and his hands, and nothing about the phone itself.

options.value: The light had gone and his hands would not hold still.
Holding it in both hands is what shook it.
options.tagChildHint: Some words tell you how two things go together. Find that word and read it again.
options.execution: Line 41 says even then, which means despite that, and this reads it as because.

rows.hintCore: Two causes, one in each line. Watch the words even then.
rows.walkScript: Read line 40 for the light, then line 41 for his hands. Two things are going against him at once. The words even then join them. They mean the second happened despite the first.

stem.text: The writer moves between tenses by a rule. What decides which he uses?

rows.key: The present is kept for what is still true, but the walk stays past.

options.value: The walk is two miles out along the sea wall to a ruined cottage.
options.tagChildHint: Some options only copy words from the passage. Ask what those words are telling you.
options.execution: A summary of what happens, which names no choice about tense at all.

options.value: He tells the whole of it the way his Nan has always told it to them.
options.tagChildHint: Sounding sensible is not enough. Find the line that proves it.
options.execution: Line 10 says her story changes each time, and at line 38 he corrects it.

options.value: Nan's part is in the present, but his own is in the past.
options.tagChildHint: Two people are being described. Check which one each detail belongs to.
options.execution: Lines 9 and 18 are his own sentences, and both are in the present.

options.value: The present is kept for what is still true, but the walk stays past.

rows.hintCore: Sort the sentences into what still stands and what happened.
rows.walkScript: Pick out the sentences in the present tense: line 8, line 18, line 37. Each one is about something that is still true today. Now check the afternoon itself. Every part of the walk is in the past.
